facts.claim: "Featherstone" was written by Samuel (Sam) Bentley. He is credited with lead vocals, guitar and keyboards on the track.
The track credits list Christina Lacy (background vocals, guitar, keyboards), David Powys (background vocals, guitar), Josh Bentley (drums, percussion) and Sam Rasmussen (bass, synthesizer).
The Paper Kites are credited as producers and recording engineers. Tim Johnston is credited as recording and mixing engineer.
The Woodland EP was recorded in early 2011 with Tim Johnston, who was one of bassist Sam Rasmussen's university teachers.
"Featherstone" was first released as a single in June 2011, ahead of the Woodland EP. The EP itself followed in August 2011.
Nettwerk Music Group put out the Woodland EP, including "Featherstone", on 5 March 2013. This was a re-release of the band's 2011 independent EP.
The song's official music video was directed by Pete Seamons and Sam Bentley.
"Featherstone" was prominently featured in the season 8 finale of Grey's Anatomy. It and "Bloom" have generated over 5 million combined YouTube views.
Sam Bentley said he felt very lucky by the online success of "Bloom" and "Featherstone".
The Paper Kites formed in Melbourne in 2009 around Sam Bentley and Christina Lacy. They expanded in 2010 with Sam Rasmussen, David Powys and Josh Bentley.

research.lineage: The song sits in the Australian (Melbourne) indie-folk tradition, built on warm harmonies and acoustic-oriented folk-pop instrumentation.

draft:
The kindest line in **Featherstone** is also its saddest: "When you go, what you leave is a work of art." Sam Bentley, who wrote the song and sings it, doesn't describe the mark a departing lover leaves as a bruise or a scar. He calls it art, and he places it on his chest and on his heart. It's a generous way to describe being hurt, and maybe a defensive one. Framing the loss as beautiful lets him keep it without having to say how much it stings.

The song is full of that kind of soft deflection. The lover drifts out into morning haze and gets lost in a tall hedge maze, an image straight out of a storybook. Then the pronouns slip. The narrator talks about "she" and then turns to address "you" directly, asking where she went and why she left. In a single verse the distance closes and the questions spill out. The chorus states the hard fact plainly: "And my love is yours but your love's not mine." There's no bitterness in it, just arithmetic. He'll go. They'll meet again down the line. They'll hate what they lost and love what they find.

Then comes the line the whole song leans on: "I'm feeling fine, we've made it to the coastline." It's hard to tell whether he means it. The second time around he adds an "oh" before the claim, a small catch that sounds like someone talking himself into it. The song never settles whether this is acceptance or a brave face, and it's better for leaving the question open. The ending gives up on words altogether, with the "ooh" refrain repeated seven times, as if whatever is left can't be put into a sentence.

The sound fits that hush. A fingerpicked acoustic guitar rolls through arpeggios at a slow, unhurried pace. Bentley's voice is breathy and close, and the production is clean, with the feel of a small room. Nothing crowds him. It's Melbourne indie-folk in its gentlest mode, acoustic folk-pop that is more interested in tenderness than in drama. The band had formed around Bentley and Christina Lacy in 2009, and they recorded the Woodland EP in early 2011 with Tim Johnston, one of bassist Sam Rasmussen's university teachers. The Paper Kites produced it themselves.

The song first came out in June 2011, and Nettwerk reissued it in 2013. Along the way it landed in the season 8 finale of *Grey's Anatomy* and found a large audience online, success that Bentley said made him feel very lucky. It's easy to hear why it travels. The song doesn't ask you to grieve loudly.

It hands you a way to say goodbye that sounds like peace, and leaves you wondering, every time that "oh" arrives, whether peace is really what you're feeling.
